details:
**Slaying the Minotaur in the Labyrinth**
Theseus's most famous feat. Because Athens owed Crete a tribute of youths and maidens after the death of King Minos's son Androgeus, Theseus volunteered to sail to Crete as one of them. There he entered the Labyrinth built by Daedalus and killed the Minotaur, the bull-headed son of Minos's wife Pasiphae and the Cretan Bull.

**Ariadne's thread and abandonment on Naxos**
Minos's daughter Ariadne fell in love with Theseus and gave him a ball of thread (and in some versions a sword) so he could find his way back out of the Labyrinth. She fled Crete with him, but Theseus abandoned her on the island of Naxos, where the god Dionysus later found and married her.

**Black sails and the death of Aegeus**
Theseus had promised his father, King Aegeus of Athens, that his ship would return with white sails if he survived. He forgot to change the black sails, and Aegeus, seeing them from a cliff, threw himself into the sea, which became known as the Aegean Sea. Theseus then became king of Athens.

**Pirithous and the Chair of Forgetfulness**
Theseus and his friend Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, descended to the underworld to abduct Persephone as a bride for Pirithous. Hades tricked them into sitting on the Chair (or Throne) of Forgetfulness (Lethe), to which they became stuck. Heracles later freed Theseus, tearing part of his thighs or buttocks off the seat (so his Athenian descendants were said to have small buttocks), but Pirithous was left behind.

**Sword and sandals under a boulder**
Before leaving Troezen, Aegeus hid his sword and sandals beneath a heavy rock, telling Theseus's mother Aethra that their son should come to Athens once he could lift it. Theseus did so, and when the sorceress Medea, then Aegeus's wife, tried to poison him at a feast, Aegeus recognized the sword and knocked the cup away. Theseus's conception had followed a Delphic oracle telling Aegeus "do not loosen the bulging mouth of the wineskin" until he reached home; Aethra slept with both Aegeus and Poseidon on the same night.

**Procrustes**
A bandit who forced travelers to fit his bed, stretching those who were too short and cutting off the limbs of those who were too long. Theseus killed him in the same way, on his own bed.

**Sinis**
The "Pine-Bender," a bandit who tied travelers between two bent pine trees and let them spring back, tearing the victims apart. Theseus killed him by his own method. Theseus fathered Melanippus with Sinis's daughter Perigune, who had hidden in a patch of asparagus.

**Sciron**
A bandit who forced travelers to wash his feet on a cliff and then kicked them into the sea, where a giant turtle ate them. Theseus threw Sciron off the cliff to the turtle. Sciron was the grandfather of Peleus, and so the great-grandfather of Achilles.

**Periphetes, the Crommyonian Sow, and Cercyon**
Other foes on Theseus's land journey from Troezen to Athens, often called his "six labors." Periphetes was a club-wielding bandit; Theseus asked to inspect his bronze club and killed him with it, keeping it as his weapon. The Crommyonian Sow (sometimes named Phaea, or an old woman of that name who owned it) was a monstrous pig, and Cercyon was a wrestler at Eleusis whom Theseus defeated in a wrestling match.

**The Marathonian Bull**
Medea sent Theseus to capture or kill the rampaging bull at Marathon (the Cretan Bull that Heracles had brought to Greece, and the father of the Minotaur), hoping it would kill him. On the way he was sheltered by the old woman Hecale, who died before he returned, so he founded honors in her memory.

**Abduction of Helen**
With Pirithous, Theseus kidnapped the young Helen of Sparta. In retaliation, her brothers the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) rescued her and carried off Theseus's mother Aethra, who was later freed by Theseus's sons Demophon and Acamas at Troy.

**Phaedra and Hippolytus**
Theseus's second wife Phaedra, the sister of Ariadne, was cursed by Aphrodite to fall in love with her stepson Hippolytus, Theseus's son by the Amazon queen. When Hippolytus rejected her, she accused him of rape; Theseus cursed his son, who was dragged to death by his own horses when a bull from Poseidon frightened them. This is the subject of Euripides's Hippolytus.

**Ship of Theseus**
The Athenians preserved the ship Theseus sailed to Crete and sent it on an annual sacred voyage to Delos, during which executions were banned (delaying Socrates's death, as Plato's Phaedo notes). According to Plutarch, its decaying planks were replaced one by one, inspiring the philosophical paradox of whether an object whose parts have all been replaced is still the same object.

**Retrieving Minos's ring from the sea**
On the voyage to Crete, King Minos threw a ring into the sea and challenged Theseus to prove he was a son of Poseidon. Theseus dove down and returned with the ring, along with a golden crown given to him by the sea goddess Amphitrite (or Thetis).

**Death on Skyros and Athenian hero**
Theseus was credited with the synoikismos, the unification of the villages of Attica into the single city-state of Athens. Ousted by Menestheus, he fled to the island of Skyros, where King Lycomedes pushed him off a cliff. The Athenian general Cimon later brought back his supposed bones, and the Temple of Hephaestus in Athens was long misnamed the Theseion after him.
